lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, History is the story of people like us. Today, we step through the last door. Whoosh! Hot wind blows on our faces. Golden sand dunes roll on and on under a huge blue sky. Then something pops out of a hole in the sand. It's a tiny fox with enormous ears! He says, Hi there! I'm Fen, a fennec fox. Welcome to the Desert of the Sun! Kiko looks up and asks, Will it rain later? Fen laughs. Rain? It hardly ever rains here. Hardly ever（ほとんど ～ない） means almost never. Say it with me. It hardly ever rains here. Wonderful! Then Fen gives us a shiny golden compass. It's the Sun Compass! It has six empty slots around the edge. Fen opens his little guidebook. Let's read the first page. "Welcome to the Desert of the Sun! A desert is a very dry place. It gets less than about two hundred fifty millimeters of rain in a whole year. Some deserts are hot, but some are cold. In fact, the largest desert in the world is icy Antarctica! Here, it hardly ever rains, so plants and animals must be clever to survive. Keep the Sun Compass with you. Each time you finish an important part of your journey, a sun crystal will fill one of its six slots. When all six shine, the compass will show you the way to your next adventure." How much rain does a desert get? Less than about two hundred fifty millimeters a year. What is the largest desert in the world? Antarctica. Now, phonics. Today's word part is g, e, o, geo. Geo means the earth. Geography. Graphy means write or draw, so geography is the study of places on Earth. Geology. Logy means study. Geology is the study of rocks and the ground. Geometry. Metry means measure. Geometry is the study of shapes. Next time, we will camp in the desert and feel a hot day and a very cold night!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, It hardly ever rains here. Today, Fen leads us to a little camp between two sand dunes. The afternoon sun is burning, and the sand is too hot to touch. Haru looks at the thermometer. Wow! It's forty-two degrees! We sit in the shade of the tent and drink lots of water. Then the sun goes down. The sky turns orange, pink, and purple. Soon, thousands of stars come out, but we start to shiver. Brr! Now we need jackets and blankets! Fen says, In the desert, it's very hot during the day, but cold at night. Say it with me. It's very hot during the day, but cold at night. Great! Riko asks, Why does it get so cold? Fen explains. The air here is very dry, and there are no clouds. Clouds and wet air work like a blanket. Without them, the heat of the day escapes into the sky. Before bed, Haru writes in his diary. Let's read it. "Day One in the Desert. This afternoon, it was over forty degrees. My water bottle felt like hot tea! We stayed in the shade and didn't run around. At sunset, everything changed. The wind became cool, and the temperature dropped very fast. Fen says desert nights can get close to zero degrees. Now I'm wearing my jacket, two pairs of socks, and a hat. But the stars are amazing. I have never seen so many stars in my life!" How hot was it in the afternoon? Over forty degrees. Why is Haru wearing two pairs of socks? Because the night is very cold. Now, phonics. Geo means the earth, and today we meet some geo people. Geographer. Take the y off geography and add e, r. It means a person who studies geography. Geologist. A geologist studies rocks and the ground. Geoscientist. A geoscientist studies the whole Earth, its land, water, and air. Next time, we will find water in the middle of the desert!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, It's very hot during the day, but cold at night. Today, we walk across the desert with Fen. Crunch, crunch. Kiko is surprised. The ground here isn't soft sand. It's hard rock and small stones called gravel. Fen says, Many people think deserts are all sand, but most of the Sahara is rock and gravel. Then Haru shouts, Look! Trees! In front of us, there are tall palm trees, green grass, and a small blue pond. Birimo rubs his eyes. Is it a dream? Fen says, No, it's an oasis! An oasis is a place where water comes out. Say it with me. An oasis is a place where water comes out. Perfect! Riko asks, But where does the water come from? It hardly ever rains here. Fen points down at his feet. It comes from under the ground. Next to the pond, there is a wooden sign. Let's read it. "Welcome to the Oasis! You are standing at a place where water comes out of the ground. Deep under the sand and rocks, there is water. Here, it rises up as a spring. People also dig wells to get it. Thanks to this water, date palms grow tall, and their sweet fruit has fed travelers for thousands of years. Please keep the water clean, and never waste it. Every drop is a gift." Where does the water at the oasis come from? From under the ground. What trees grow at the oasis? Date palms. Now, phonics. Today, geo meets some new friends. Geothermal. Thermal means heat, so geothermal means the heat inside the earth. Japan's hot springs get their heat from inside the earth. Geopark. A geopark is a park where you can learn about the earth, like rocks, volcanoes, and coasts. Geoglyph. A geoglyph is a giant picture drawn on the ground. The Nazca Lines in Peru are famous geoglyphs. Next time, Fen will show us a big climate map of the whole world!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, An oasis is a place where water comes out. Today, a strong wind is blowing sand everywhere, so we stay inside Fen's big tent. Fen rolls out a huge map of the world. It's covered in colors: yellow, green, white, and dark green. Fen says, This is my climate map. Climate means the usual weather in a place over many years. Haru points to the dark green part. What's the weather like here? Fen says, That's the rainforest. It's hot and rainy all year. Some places are rainy all year. Say it with me. Some places are rainy all year. Wonderful! Kiko finds Japan. It's light green. Fen says, Some places have four seasons, like Japan. Let's read the key on the map. "Climate Map Key. Dark green: rainforest. It is hot and rainy all year, and tall trees grow very close together. The Amazon rainforest in South America is the largest one. Yellow: desert. It is dry all year. Some deserts, like the Sahara, are hot. Others, like the Gobi in Asia, have very cold winters. Light green: four seasons. Summers are warm, winters are cool or cold, and it rains in many months. White: polar. It is freezing all year, and the land is covered with ice and snow." What's the weather like in the rainforest? It's hot and rainy all year. Which desert has very cold winters? The Gobi. Is this a fact or an opinion? Japan has the best climate in the world. Riko thinks so, but it's an opinion! Now, phonics. Today, geo words get new endings. Geographic. Take the y off geography and add i, c. Now it's a describing word. A geographic map shows mountains, rivers, and deserts. Geometric. Geometric shapes are circles, triangles, and squares. Look, Fen's tent has a geometric pattern! Geode. A geode is a round rock. It looks plain on the outside, but inside, it's full of sparkling crystals. Next time, we will give a climate report about deserts around the world!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Some places are rainy all year. Today is Climate Report Day! Fen sits on a flat rock, and his big ears stand straight up. He's ready to listen. Riko goes first. She points to the map and says, The Sahara is located in North Africa. It's hot and dry. Located tells us where something is on the map. Say it with me. The Sahara is located in North Africa. It's hot and dry. Wonderful! Next, Haru talks about a very different desert. Antarctica is the largest desert. It's cold and dry. Kiko asks, Where is the Gobi Desert located? Birimo answers, It's located in Asia, in Mongolia and China. Let's read Riko's report. "Climate Report: Deserts of the World. Deserts get very little rain, but they are not all the same. The Sahara is located in North Africa. It is the largest hot desert, and it's almost as big as the United States. The Atacama Desert is located in Chile, in South America. It is one of the driest places on Earth. Some parts hardly ever get any rain at all. The Gobi Desert is located in Asia. Its summers can be hot, but its winters are very cold. Antarctica is the largest desert of all. It's cold and dry, and it's covered with ice." Which desert is one of the driest places on Earth? The Atacama Desert. How big is the Sahara? It's almost as big as the United States. Fen claps his paws. Amazing reports, everyone! Suddenly, the Sun Compass grows warm in Haru's hands. A tiny golden light appears. Click! The first sun crystal drops into a slot! It shines like a little sun. Now, phonics. Let's review our geo words. Geography, the study of places. Geologist, a person who studies rocks. Geothermal, the heat inside the earth. Geometric, with shapes like triangles and circles. Next time, we will meet a kind old camel and ride with his caravan!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The Sahara is located in North Africa. It's hot and dry. Today, we hear bells. Ding, ding, ding. A long line of camels is walking over the dunes. It's a caravan! At the front, there is a big old camel with a gentle smile. He kneels down slowly and says, Good morning, little travelers. I'm Humphrey. I lead this caravan. Hop on! We climb onto the camels. Whoa! They stand up back legs first, and we almost fall off! Later, Haru asks, Humphrey, aren't you thirsty? Humphrey smiles. Not yet. Camels can go many days without water. Say it with me. Camels can go many days without water. Great! Kiko asks, Is there water in your hump? Humphrey shakes his head. Our humps store fat, not water. Humphrey carries a fact card in his saddle bag. Let's read it. "Camel Fact Card. Camels are amazing desert travelers. They can go about a week or more without water. When they finally find water, they can drink about one hundred liters at one time! Their humps store fat, not water. Long eyelashes protect their eyes, and they can close their noses to keep sand out. Their wide feet don't sink in soft sand. They also have tough mouths, so they can eat thorny desert plants. Some people call camels the ships of the desert." How much water can a camel drink at one time? About one hundred liters. What do camels' humps store? Fat. Is this a fact or an opinion? Camels are the best animals in the world. It's an opinion, but Humphrey likes it! Now, phonics. Today's ending is a, l. Al turns a word into a describing word. Nature, natural. Drop the e, and nay becomes a short a, like in cat. Nation, national. The short a again. Tropic, tropical. Tropical places are hot and wet. Next time, we will watch desert animals, and Fen will tell us the secret of his big ears!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Camels can go many days without water. Today, Humphrey's caravan stops near some big rocks. Fen whispers, Shh. Let's watch the desert animals. A little lizard runs quickly across the hot sand. Then Riko looks at Fen. Fen, why are your ears so big? Fen laughs. My ears are my air conditioners! Heat leaves my body through them. Desert foxes have big ears so that they can stay cool. So that（～できるように） tells us what something is for. Say it with me. Desert foxes have big ears so that they can stay cool. Perfect! Fen turns his ears this way and that way. They help me hear bugs moving under the sand, too. Dinner! Haru asks, Why are your feet so furry? Fen says, So that I can walk on hot sand. Let's read a page from Fen's animal notebook. "How Desert Animals Survive. I'm a fennec fox, the smallest fox in the world. My huge ears let heat out of my body so that I can stay cool. They also help me hear insects under the sand. My feet are covered with fur so that I can walk on hot sand. During the day, I sleep in a cool burrow under the ground. At night, when the air is cooler, I go out to hunt. My friend Humphrey has long eyelashes so that sand can't get into his eyes." Why does Fen have furry feet? So that he can walk on hot sand. When does Fen hunt? At night. Now, phonics. Let's add a, l again. Coast, coastal. A coastal town is a town by the sea. Season, seasonal. Seasonal fruit comes only in one season, like watermelon in summer. Center, central. Drop the e from e, r, and add a, l. Central means in the middle. Fen's burrow has a central room, and it's cool inside! Next time, we will visit a garden of tall, spiky cactus plants!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Desert foxes have big ears so that they can stay cool. Today, Fen takes us to a cactus garden. Some cactus plants are round like balls. Some are flat like pancakes. And one is taller than a house! Its green arms point up to the sky. Haru touches a spine. Ouch! Fen laughs. Be careful! Then Fen points to a thick green stem. It's full of water inside, like a sponge. A cactus stores water in its thick stem. Say it with me. A cactus stores water in its thick stem. Wonderful! Kiko asks, But where are its leaves? Fen points to the spines. Its spines are special leaves. Riko asks, Why does a cactus have spines? Fen says, To lose less water and to keep animals away. Let's read the sign in front of the tallest cactus. "The Saguaro Cactus. This giant can grow taller than twelve meters and live for more than one hundred fifty years. Like other cactus plants, it stores water in its thick stem. After a rain, the stem gets fatter. Its spines are special leaves. They lose much less water than big flat leaves, they protect the cactus from hungry animals, and they even make a little shade. Waxy skin keeps the water inside. The roots are wide and shallow, so they can catch rain quickly before it dries up." How tall can a saguaro grow? Taller than twelve meters. What do the spines do? They lose less water, protect the cactus, and make a little shade. Now, phonics. A, l makes describing words. Globe, global. Drop the e and add a, l. Global means all around the world. Culture, cultural. Drop the e again. Cultural things are about the way people live, like food and festivals. Origin, original. An original idea is new, your very own. The cactus has an original way to save water! Next time, the Sun Compass will show us pictures of icy lands!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, A cactus stores water in its thick stem. Today, the Sun Compass starts to glow. A picture appears in the air above it. It's white and icy! Kiko says, Brr! That's the opposite of the desert! Fen says, The compass wants us to compare. Let's see how animals live in cold places. In the picture, emperor penguins stand on the ice in Antarctica. Fen says, Penguins have thick feathers to keep warm. Say it with me. Penguins have thick feathers to keep warm. Great! Look! The penguins are standing very close together. Emperor penguins huddle together in order to keep warm. In order to means the same as to here, but it sounds a little more formal. Then the picture changes to the Arctic. An Arctic fox is walking in the snow. Fen says, Look at its ears! They're so small! Let's read the card under the picture. "Animals in Cold Places. Emperor penguins live in Antarctica. They have thick, tightly packed feathers and a layer of fat to keep warm. In storms, they huddle together in order to share their heat. Polar bears live in the Arctic. Their thick fur, black skin, and a layer of fat keep the cold out. The Arctic fox has small ears and thick fur to keep heat in. In winter, its fur turns white, so it can hide in the snow. Desert animals let heat out. Cold-place animals keep heat in." Why do emperor penguins huddle together? In order to share their heat. What color is the Arctic fox's fur in winter? White. Fen laughs. My ears let heat out, and its ears keep heat in. We're cousins with opposite ears! Now, phonics. More a, l words! Environment, environmental. Environmental means about nature and the world around us. Music, musical. A musical is a show with lots of songs. Person, personal. Personal means about one person, like your personal diary. Next time, we will hold an adaptation fair!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Penguins have thick feathers to keep warm. Today is the Adaptation Fair at the oasis! Fen explains. Adaptation means the special body parts and habits that help an animal live in its home. Every table has a poster and a quiz. Riko's poster is about Fen and his big ears. Birimo's poster shows a giant cactus. Then Haru holds up his poster with a picture hidden under a cloth. He says, This animal has wide feet so that it can walk on soft sand. Say it with me. This animal has wide feet so that it can walk on soft sand. Wonderful! Kiko shouts, What animal is it? Is it a camel? Behind us, someone laughs. It's Humphrey! He says, Yes, it's me! Let's read Haru's quiz poster. "Guess the Animal! This animal lives in hot, dry deserts. It has wide feet so that it can walk on soft sand. Its long eyelashes keep sand out of its eyes, and it can close its nose in a sandstorm. It can go many days without water, and its hump stores fat, not water. Its tough mouth can even eat thorny plants. Some people call it the ship of the desert. Can you guess? Hint: he leads our caravan!" What helps this animal walk on soft sand? Its wide feet. What does its hump store? Fat. Humphrey bows his long neck. What a wonderful fair! Fen's ears turn pink with joy. Then the Sun Compass glows again. Click! The second sun crystal drops into its slot. Now we have two crystals! Now, phonics. Let's review. Natural. Nature becomes natural with a, l. Seasonal. Season plus a, l. Global. Drop the e from globe and add a, l. And one geo word. Geopark, a park where we learn about the earth. Next time, we will learn north, south, east, and west, and read a map with a compass!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This animal has wide feet so that it can walk on soft sand. Today, the sun is just coming up over our desert camp. Fen runs out of the tent with a big roll of paper. Good morning, explorers! Let's learn to read a map! Fen unrolls the map on the sand and holds up the Sun Compass. It has two shining crystals and a little gold needle. The needle points north. North is at the top of the map. South is at the bottom. East is on the right, and west is on the left. Fen taps a small blue circle. Here's the oasis. And here's our camp. Which way is the oasis? Kiko looks carefully. The oasis is to the east of the camp. Say it with me. The oasis is to the east of the camp. Wonderful! Haru points at the rising sun. That's east, too! The sun rises in the east and sets in the west. Let's read the notes on Fen's map. "Fen's Camp Map. North of the camp, there are rocky hills. Don't climb them in the afternoon, because the rocks get very hot. South of the camp, there are tall sand dunes. They change shape when the wind blows. The oasis is to the east of the camp, about one hour on foot. An old stone road starts to the west of the camp and leads to the western edge of the desert. Always carry water, and always check your compass!" What is to the south of the camp? Tall sand dunes. Why shouldn't you climb the hills in the afternoon? Because the rocks get very hot. Now, phonics. Add e, r, n to a direction, and it means in that direction or in that part. North, northern. South, southern. Listen! We say SUH-thern, not south-ern. East, eastern. West, western. Next time, we will look at a map of the whole desert country.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The oasis is to the east of the camp. Today, Fen brings an even bigger map. It shows the whole desert country, and it covers the floor of the tent! Fen says, Let's be geographers today! A geographer studies places and explains maps. Look at the top of the map. There are tall, gray mountains with snow on their tops. Riko says, The mountains are located in the north. Say it with me. The mountains are located in the north. Great! Located means where something is. Haru finds a long blue line. Where is the river? Fen says, It's located in the eastern part of the country. It starts in the mountains and flows south. Kiko finds lots of tiny yellow waves in the bottom left corner. Those are the biggest sand dunes, says Fen. They are in the southwest. Let's read the box on the side of the map. "Welcome to the Desert Country! This country has high mountains, a long river, and a huge sea of sand. The mountains are located in the north. In winter, snow sometimes falls on them. When the snow melts in spring, the water flows into the river. The river runs through the eastern part of the country, so most farms and towns are there. The biggest sand dunes are in the southwest. Hardly anyone lives there, but the stars at night are amazing." Why are most towns in the east? Because the river is there. Where does the river water come from? From the snow on the mountains. Now, phonics. When we put two directions together, north or south always comes first. Northeast. Southeast. Northwest. Southwest. We never say east-north! The sand dunes are in the southwest corner, and the mountains stretch from the northwest to the northeast. Next time, Fen will spin a giant globe, and we will travel around the whole world!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The mountains are located in the north. Today, Fen rolls a giant globe into the tent. It's as tall as Birimo! Fen gives it a push, and the whole world spins round and round. Blue, green, brown, white. Stop! Look at all this land. These huge pieces of land are called continents. Let's count them together. Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, and Australia. There are seven continents. Say it with me. There are seven continents. Perfect! Asia is the largest continent. Haru finds Japan. It's a small island country in East Asia. Kiko asks, How many oceans are there? Fen says, There are five. The Pacific is the largest. Let's read the little guidebook that comes with the globe. "Our Blue and Green Planet. There are seven continents and five oceans on Earth. The oceans are the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern, and the Arctic. The Pacific Ocean is so big that all the continents could fit inside it. Africa is home to the Sahara, the largest hot desert in the world. Antarctica is covered with ice, but it's a desert, too, because very little snow or rain falls there. In fact, it's the largest desert on Earth!" Which ocean is the largest? The Pacific. Why is Antarctica a desert? Because very little snow or rain falls there. Now, phonics. W, a, r, d means toward. It sounds like word, but we spell it w, a, r, d. Northward. Southward. Eastward. Westward. If you fly eastward from Japan, you cross the Pacific Ocean and reach North America. If you fly southward, you reach Australia. Next time, Fen has a quiz for us. Where in the world is it?

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, There are seven continents. Today, Fen puts on a tiny bow tie and holds up a little bell. Ding, ding! Welcome to Where in the World? Listen to the hints and guess the country! Everyone gets ready. Hint one. It's the largest country on its continent. Hint two. It has the biggest rainforest in the world, the Amazon. Hint three. It's a country in South America. Say it with me. It's a country in South America. Wonderful! Haru presses the buzzer. Is it Brazil? Yes! Ding, ding, ding! Now, let's read the next quiz card. "Quiz Card Number Two. This country is in South America, too. Part of it is a dry desert near the sea. Long ago, people drew giant pictures on the ground there. There is a monkey, a hummingbird, and a spider. The pictures are so big that you can see them best from an airplane or a hill. People still wonder why they were made. Which country is it?" Riko knows! It's Peru! These pictures are called the Nazca Lines. Where can you see them best? From an airplane or a hill. Then Fen asks one more question. Where is Egypt? Kiko says, It's in Africa. The Nile flows through it. And there are pyramids! Ding, ding! Fen laughs and spins around. What a smart team! Now, phonics. Ward means toward, again. Upward. Look upward at the sky. Downward. Look downward at the sand. Forward. Take one step forward. Backward. Take one step backward. Remember, all four words end with w, a, r, d. Next time, we will follow an old treasure map to find a secret well!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, It's a country in South America. Today, Fen finds an old, yellow piece of paper inside a clay jar. It's a treasure map! At the top, it says, The Old Well. Fen's huge ears stand straight up. Long ago, travelers drank from this well, but now nobody remembers where it is. Can you guide us? Haru reads the first line. Start at the three palm trees. Then he points to a long arrow. Go north for two kilometers. You'll see the well. Say it with me. Go north for two kilometers. You'll see the well. Wonderful! Kiko checks the Sun Compass. North is this way! Let's read the whole map. "The Way to the Old Well. Start at the three palm trees on the southern side of the oasis. Walk westward until you reach a big red rock. It looks like a sleeping camel. Turn north at the big red rock. Go north for two kilometers. You'll see the well. It is located between two small hills. If the wind is strong, cover your face and walk slowly. A good traveler always checks the compass!" Where do you turn north? At the big red rock. What does the rock look like? A sleeping camel. We walk and walk across the hot sand. Then Riko shouts, Look! Two small hills, and a circle of old stones between them! It's the well! Haru pulls up the bucket. Cool, clear water! Suddenly the Sun Compass glows. Click! The third sun crystal clicks into its slot. Three crystals now! Now, phonics. Let's review. Southern. Remember, SUH-thern. Northeast. North comes first. Westward. Toward the west, spelled w, a, r, d. Coastal. Coast plus a, l. Geographer. A geographer studies places, just like our great map readers! Next time, we will visit a weather station and meet a scientist who loves graphs!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Go north for two kilometers. You'll see the well. Today, we walk to a little white building on a hill. There's a spinning wind cup on the roof and a big thermometer by the door. It's a weather station! A woman with sandy boots and a big smile opens the door. Welcome! I'm Dr. Mira Sands. I study desert weather, and I love graphs! Dr. Mira points to a poster on the wall. A red line goes up and down across it. The graph shows the temperature in July. Say it with me. The graph shows the temperature in July. Wonderful! Look at the red line. It goes up and down like sand dunes. What was the highest temperature? It was forty-six degrees! Let's read Dr. Mira's weather notes. "July Weather Notes. The graph shows the highest temperature on each day in July. Every day was hotter than forty degrees. The hottest day was July twentieth. It was forty-six degrees, and even the lizards stayed in the shade! The coolest day was July third, when clouds covered the sky. It never rained this month. Tip: In July, drink lots of water and stay inside in the afternoon." What was the hottest day? July twentieth. Why was July third cooler? Because clouds covered the sky. Now, phonics. Let's read big numbers. Dr. Mira's station is three hundred fifty meters above sea level. Three, five, zero. Three hundred fifty. She has four thousand photos of clouds. Four, comma, zero, zero, zero. Four thousand. Her weather balloon flies higher than twelve thousand meters. One, two, comma, zero, zero, zero. Twelve thousand. And sixty thousand people read her weather report every month. Six, zero, comma, zero, zero, zero. Sixty thousand. Remember, no s on hundred or thousand! Next time, we will look at a graph of visitors to a desert park.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The graph shows the temperature in July. Today, Dr. Mira takes us to the gate of Sunrise Desert Park. Lots of people are waiting in line with big hats and water bottles. Dr. Mira opens her laptop and shows us a bar graph. Each bar is one year. Look! The bars get taller and taller. The number of visitors increased. Say it with me. The number of visitors increased. Wonderful! Increased means it went up. Decreased means it went down. Kiko points to one short bar. Did it go up or down here? Dr. Mira says, It decreased a little in the stormy year. There were many big sandstorms, so fewer people came. Then Haru finds another graph. The number of camels in the park stayed the same, about fifty every year. Let's read the park's report. "Sunrise Desert Park: Ten Years of Visitors. Ten years ago, the park was very quiet. Only two hundred fifty thousand people visited. Then the park opened a star-watching tour and a camel trail, and more and more people came. Three years ago, there were many sandstorms, and the number of visitors decreased a little. But last year, one million people visited! Now the park asks everyone to stay on the trails so that the desert plants stay safe." How many people visited ten years ago? Two hundred fifty thousand. Why did more people come? Because the park opened a star-watching tour and a camel trail. Now, phonics. Big, big numbers! Two hundred fifty thousand. Two, five, zero, comma, zero, zero, zero. One million. One, and then six zeros. When you see two commas, think million! Three million. The park's website had three million visits last year. Eight million. And its funny camel video was watched eight million times! Next time, we will count the animals at the oasis.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The number of visitors increased. Today, Dr. Mira takes us back to the oasis. Every morning, animals come to drink at the pond, and Dr. Mira counts them. She writes the numbers in a table. Let's look. Goats, sixty. Camels, forty. Horses, twenty. Riko says, Forty is two times twenty. So there are twice as many camels as horses. Say it with me. There are twice as many camels as horses. Wonderful! Haru thinks hard. And there are three times as many goats as horses! Kiko adds them up. Sixty plus forty plus twenty is one hundred twenty animals. Half of the animals are goats! Let's read Dr. Mira's notebook. "Animals at the Oasis, Monday Morning. Today, one hundred twenty animals came to drink. Half of them were goats. They pushed, jumped, and made a lot of noise. One third of the animals were camels. There were twice as many camels as horses. The camels drank slowly and quietly. One quarter of the camels were babies, and they stayed close to their mothers. The horses came last, when the sun was already high." How many animals came to drink? One hundred twenty. Which animals were the noisiest? The goats. Now, phonics. Let's read fractions. One half. One, slash, two. Half of the animals are goats. One quarter. One, slash, four. One quarter of the camels are babies. Three quarters. Three, slash, four. Three quarters of the camels are grown-ups. When the top number is two or more, add an s. One third. One, slash, three. One third of the animals are camels. Fractions help us talk about parts of a whole. Next time, Dr. Mira will show us a round chart of all the land on Earth. It looks like a pizza!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, There are twice as many camels as horses. Today, Dr. Mira draws a big circle on the whiteboard and cuts it into slices. It looks like a pizza! This is a pie chart, she says. The whole circle is all the land on Earth. Each slice shows one part. Look at this big yellow slice. It shows the deserts, hot ones and cold ones. It's about one third of the circle. About thirty percent of the land is desert. Say it with me. About thirty percent of the land is desert. Wonderful! Percent means out of one hundred. Thirty percent means thirty out of every one hundred. Then Dr. Mira draws a second circle. This one shows the whole surface of Earth, and most of it is blue. About seventy percent of Earth's surface is water. Let's read the poster next to the whiteboard. "Our Water Planet. About seventy percent of Earth's surface is water, but almost all of it is salty sea water. Only about three percent of Earth's water is fresh water, and most of that is frozen ice. So the water we can drink is very, very special. People in the desert know this well. They never waste a single drop. Wherever we live, we can learn from them and save water, too." How much of Earth's water is fresh water? Only about three percent. Is this a fact or an opinion? Most fresh water is frozen ice. It's a fact. Now, phonics. Thirty percent. Three, zero, and the percent sign. Seventy-five percent. Seven, five, and the percent sign. In Dr. Mira's town, seventy-five percent of the rain falls in winter. Two point five. Two, dot, five. We say point for the dot. In March, two point five millimeters of rain fell. Zero point five. Zero, dot, five. In May, only zero point five millimeters fell. That's a tiny drop! Next time, we will give our own graph presentations!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, About thirty percent of the land is desert. Today is Graph Presentation Day at Dr. Mira's weather station! Fen sits in the front row, big ears up, ready to listen. Haru goes first. The graph shows the temperature in July. Every day was hotter than forty degrees! Riko is next. The number of visitors to the desert park increased to one million. Birimo shows the animal table. There are twice as many camels as horses! Then it's Kiko's turn. She holds up a bar graph with twelve blue bars. This graph shows the rain in our desert town. As you can see, it hardly ever rains in summer. Say it with me. This graph shows the rain in our desert town. As you can see, it hardly ever rains in summer. Wonderful! As you can see is a great way to point to your graph. Let's read Kiko's presentation notes. "Rain in Our Desert Town. This graph shows the rain in our desert town. Each bar shows one month. The tallest bar is January, with twenty-five millimeters. As you can see, it hardly ever rains in summer. In June, July, and August, there was no rain at all. About one hundred millimeters fell in the whole year. That's less than two hundred fifty millimeters, so our town is a real desert! Thank you for listening. Do you have any questions?" Which month had the most rain? January. Why is the town a real desert? Because it gets less than two hundred fifty millimeters of rain a year. Dr. Mira claps. Wonderful graphs! Then the Sun Compass glows. Click! The fourth sun crystal clicks into place. Four crystals now! Now, phonics. Let's review. Thirty percent. One half. One million, with six zeros. Western. West plus e, r, n. National. Nation plus a, l. Listen. Nation, national. Next time, we will visit Palm Village and learn why every drop of water counts.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This graph shows the rain in our desert town. As you can see, it hardly ever rains in summer. Today, Fen leads us across the hot sand to Palm Village. In the middle of the village, there is an old stone well. A long line of people waits beside it with buckets and clay jars. An old woman slowly pulls up the rope. Splash! Cool, clear water fills her bucket. Nobody spills a drop. Fen's big ears twitch. He whispers, Here, every drop counts. Water is precious in the desert. Say it with me. Water is precious in the desert. Wonderful! Precious means very important and hard to get, like treasure. Riko asks, Why is water so precious? Fen says, It hardly ever rains here. Let's read the sign next to the well. "Welcome to the Palm Village Well. This well is very old and very deep. The water comes from under the ground, far below the sand. Our village gets less than 100 millimeters of rain a year, so this well is our life. Please take only what you need. Close the lid after you use the well, so that sand and animals stay out. Thank you for helping us. Water is precious, so let's not waste a single drop!" Where does the water come from? From under the ground. Why should you close the lid? So that sand and animals stay out. Is this a fact or an opinion? Water is precious. It's an opinion, but in the desert, everyone shares it! Now, phonics. Today's ending is a, g, e. It sounds like the end of bridge, but we spell it a, g, e. Average. Percentage. Storage. Shortage. Storage is a place to keep things, like a big water tank. A shortage means there is not enough. When the rain doesn't come, the village has a water shortage. Next time, we visit a lake that is getting smaller.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Water is precious in the desert. Today, Dr. Mira Sands takes us to Mirror Lake. Long ago, the lake was so smooth and wide that it looked like a giant mirror. But now, we see a ring of white, cracked mud all around it. The water is far away from the old shore. Haru points to a big rock. Look! There's an old water line up here! Dr. Mira nods and shows us her temperature graph. Every summer this lake gets hotter and hotter. The hot sun turns the water into vapor, and it goes up into the air. Because of the heat, the lake became smaller. Say it with me. Because of the heat, the lake became smaller. Great! Because of comes before a thing, like the heat or the rain. Let's read Dr. Mira's notebook. "Mirror Lake Notes. Ten years ago, Mirror Lake was about two kilometers wide. Now, it is less than one kilometer wide. Why? First, the summers here have become hotter. Because of the heat, a lot of water goes up into the air every day. Second, it hardly ever rained this year. Third, more and more farms take water from the lake. Because of the dry weather, many plants on the shore turned brown. The fish and birds have fewer places to live now. We must take care of this lake." How wide was the lake ten years ago? About two kilometers. Give one reason why the lake became smaller. The summers became hotter, it hardly ever rained, or farms took water. Now, phonics. Today's ending is u, r, e. Listen. Temperature. Measure. Pressure. Moisture. The ending sounds like the end of picture or treasure, but we always spell it u, r, e. We measure the temperature with a thermometer. Moisture means a little water in the air or in the ground. Next time, we hear the story of a village that became green again.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Because of the heat, the lake became smaller. Today, Fen takes us over a tall sand dune. At the top, we stop and stare. Below us, there is a green valley full of trees, fields, and flowers! Birds are singing everywhere. Fen says, Welcome to Green Valley. Forty years ago, this place was brown and dusty. Then the people had an idea. People planted trees. As a result, the village became green again. Say it with me. People planted trees. As a result, the village became green again. Perfect! As a result tells us what happened next because of something. Let's read the story board in the village square. "The Story of Green Valley. Forty years ago, Green Valley was dry and brown. Strong winds blew sand into the fields, and the crops died. Many families had to leave. Then the villagers made a plan. They planted long rows of trees around the village. The trees stopped the wind and gave shade. Their roots held the soil in place. As a result, the fields stayed soft and wet, and the crops grew again. Then the birds came back, too. Today, Green Valley is green again!" Why did the crops die? Because of strong winds that blew sand into the fields. What happened after the trees grew? The fields stayed soft and wet, and the crops grew again. Green Valley is a story village, but this happens in the real world, too. In Africa, many countries are planting a Great Green Wall of trees across the Sahel, south of the Sahara, to stop the desert from spreading. Now, phonics. Today's ending is e, a, s, e. It sounds like the end of geese. Increase. Decrease. Release. When the number of trees increases, it goes up. When it decreases, it goes down. Release means let something go. Release the bird, and it flies free! Next time, we find out how much water we use in a day.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, People planted trees. As a result, the village became green again. Today, we are back at our camp. Dr. Mira Sands puts a big bottle on the table. It holds two liters of water. She asks, How much water do you use at home in one day? Haru guesses, Ten bottles? Kiko guesses, Fifty bottles? Dr. Mira smiles and shakes her head. In Japan, one person uses about 200 liters of water a day at home. That's a hundred of these bottles! So, We use about 200 liters of water a day. Say it with me. We use about 200 liters of water a day. Wonderful! Birimo's eyes go round. A hundred bottles? Where does it all go? Let's read Dr. Mira's water chart. "Where Does Our Water Go? In Japan, one person uses about 200 liters of water a day at home. A shower uses about 12 liters a minute, so a five-minute shower uses about 60 liters. A newer toilet uses about 5 liters a flush. If you flush five times, that's about 25 liters. If you leave the tap running while you brush your teeth for 30 seconds, about 6 liters go down the drain. We also use water for cooking, washing dishes, and doing laundry." How much water does a five-minute shower use? About 60 liters. How much water does a newer toilet use in one flush? About 5 liters. Riko says, Leaving the tap running for 30 seconds wastes about 6 liters. That's three of these bottles! Now, phonics. Today's ending is o, u, n, t. It sounds like ount. Amount. Count. Account. Count means say the numbers, one, two, three. Amount means how much of something there is, like the amount of water in a bottle. An account is a report of what happened. Next time, we start a save-water campaign in Palm Village!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, We use about 200 liters of water a day. Today is a big day. We are presenting our Save Water Campaign in the square of Palm Village. Fen, Dr. Mira, and many villagers sit on colorful rugs in the shade of the palm trees. Kiko holds up our poster. It has a big blue drop on it. Haru steps forward and says, We can save water by turning off the tap. Say it with me. We can save water by turning off the tap. Wonderful! By plus ing tells us how we do it. Riko asks, How else can we save water? Birimo says, We can take shorter showers. Let's read our campaign poster. "Every Drop Counts! Join Our Save Water Campaign. One: Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. You can save about 6 liters every 30 seconds. Two: Take shorter showers. One minute less saves about 12 liters. Three: Use the water from washing vegetables to water the plants. Four: Collect rainwater on rainy days. Five: If you see a leaky tap, tell an adult. Our goal is to cut our water use by one quarter. Small actions add up. Let's do it together!" How much water can you save if your shower is one minute shorter? About 12 liters. What should you do if you see a leaky tap? Tell an adult. The villagers clap and cheer. Fen's big ears stand straight up. Then the Sun Compass begins to glow. Click! The fifth sun crystal clicks into place! Only one slot is empty now. Now, phonics. Let's review. Average ends like bridge. Temperature ends like picture. Increase ends like geese. Amount ends like count. One quarter. One, slash, four. That means one of four equal parts. Next time, we read a desert story about a girl who found water.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, We can save water by turning off the tap. Tonight, we sit around a campfire under the stars. Fen pulls a small, sandy book out of his bag. He says, Everyone in the desert knows this story. Remember, it's a made-up story. Lina is not a real girl, but her story is like many true stories from dry places. Fen opens the book, and I say, Read the story of a girl who found water. Say it with me. Read the story of a girl who found water. Very good! Let's read it together. "Lina lived in a small village in the eastern part of a dry valley. It hardly ever rained there, and the old well was almost empty. Every morning, Lina walked for an hour to get water. One day at sunrise, she saw something strange at the dry riverbed. Green plants were growing there, and little birds were hopping around them. But there was no water anywhere. Lina thought, Plants need water. Maybe there is water under the ground! She ran back and told the villagers. They dug and dug. At last, cool water came up. Because of Lina's sharp eyes, the village had water again." Why did Lina think there was water? Because she saw green plants and birds. What did the villagers do? They dug, and they found water. What is the lesson of the story? Look carefully, and you can find answers. Now, phonics. Let's review. Geology. Geo means earth, and logy means study. Geologists study rocks and the ground. Original. Origin plus a, l. Eastern. East plus e, r, n. Lina's village was in the eastern part of the valley. One third. One, slash, three. One of three equal parts. Moisture. The plants found moisture under the sand. Next time, it's the Geography Quiz Rally around the oasis!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Read the story of a girl who found water. Today is the Geography Quiz Rally! Fen has hidden five quiz cards around the oasis. We run from station to station with our rally cards. At the first station, under the tallest palm tree, Fen's ears pop up from behind the trunk. He asks, Which is the largest desert? Say it with me. Which is the largest desert? Great! Haru shouts, Is it the Sahara? Fen giggles. No, it's Antarctica. It's a cold desert. It gets very little rain or snow. Riko asks, Which is the largest hot desert? Fen says, The Sahara. It's almost as big as the United States. Let's read our rally card. "Geography Quiz Rally Card. Station 1, the tallest palm tree: Which is the largest desert? Station 2, the old well: Which desert in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth? Station 3, the camel tent: Is most of the Sahara sand, or rock and gravel? Station 4, the cactus garden: In which country can you see the Nazca Lines? Station 5, the big rock: Which ocean is the largest? Get a stamp at each station. Five stamps win a date cookie!" Which desert is one of the driest places on Earth? The Atacama Desert in Chile. Is most of the Sahara sand? No, most of it is rock and gravel. And the answers to Stations 4 and 5? Peru and the Pacific Ocean! Now, phonics. Let's review. Geoglyph. Geo means earth. A geoglyph is a giant picture drawn on the ground, like the Nazca Lines in Peru. Tropical. Tropic plus a, l. Southwest. South comes first. Twelve thousand. One, two, comma, zero zero zero. No s on thousand. Haru walked twelve thousand steps in the rally! Shortage. Short plus a, g, e. In the desert, there is often a water shortage. Next time, we write our own graph reports.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Which is the largest desert? Today, we visit Dr. Mira's little weather station again. She gives each of us a sheet of paper and a pencil. Today, you are all scientists, she says. Let's write graph reports. She pins a graph on the wall. It shows the trees in Green Valley. The line starts low and climbs up, up, up. Kiko reads it out loud. The graph shows the number of trees in the village. It increased from 100 to 900. Say it with me. The graph shows the number of trees in the village. It increased from 100 to 900. Perfect! Dr. Mira says, Here is a model report. Let's read it. "My Graph Report: Trees in Green Valley. The graph shows the number of trees in the village. It increased from 100 to 900 in ten years. As you can see, it increased the most after people dug a new well. Because of the trees, the wind is weaker and the fields are greener. As a result, more birds live there now. I think planting trees is a great idea." How many trees were there at first? One hundred. Which sentence is an opinion? I think planting trees is a great idea. Dr. Mira counts on her fingers. A good report has a title, what the graph shows, the change, the reason, the result, and your opinion. Now, it's your turn! Choose a graph and write your own report. Now, phonics. Let's review. Geoscientist. Geo means earth, so a geoscientist studies the earth. Environmental. Environment plus a, l. Forward. W, a, r, d, not w, o, r, d. Step forward! Seventy-five percent. Seven, five, and the percent sign. That's the same as three quarters. Decrease. E, a, s, e. When something decreases, it goes down. Next time, Humphrey leads our farewell caravan through the desert.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The graph shows the number of trees in the village. It increased from 100 to 900. Today, Humphrey the old camel leads our farewell caravan. Bells jingle as we sway across the golden dunes. First, we pass our old camp, where the days were hot and the nights were cold. Humphrey turns his long neck and winks. He asks, Do camels store water in their humps? Birimo answers, No, you store fat! Haru says, Camels have humps so that they can go a long time without food. Then we stop at Dr. Mira's weather station. Riko points to the thermometer graph. The graph shows how hot it is. Say it with me. Camels have humps so that they can go a long time without food. The graph shows how hot it is. Wonderful! Let's read Kiko's desert journal. "My Desert Journal. We came to the Desert of the Sun through the Corridor of Time. It hardly ever rains here, so water is precious. At the oasis, water comes up from under the ground, and date palms grow there. Fen has big ears so that he can stay cool. A cactus stores water in its thick stem. Mirror Lake became smaller because of the heat. In Green Valley, people planted trees. As a result, the village became green again. I will miss this place!" Why does Fen have big ears? So that he can stay cool. What happened in Green Valley? People planted trees, and the village became green again. Fen gives each of us a round rock. Crack! Inside, it sparkles with crystals. It's a geode! Now, phonics. Let's review. Geode. Geo means earth. Coastal. Coast plus a, l. Northwest. North comes first. Two point five. Two, dot, five. We say point for the dot. Count. O, u, n, t. Let's count our sun crystals. One, two, three, four, five! Next time, it's the World 32 Earth Festival!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Camels have humps so that they can go a long time without food. The graph shows how hot it is. Today is the World 32 Earth Festival at the oasis! Lanterns hang from the palm trees, and drums go boom, boom! Haru, Kiko, and Riko share their maps, posters, and reports. Fen, Humphrey, and Dr. Mira sit in the front row. Then Fen stands up and says, Hot deserts, cold deserts, rainforests, and icy lands. Every place is different. Every place on Earth has its own amazing story. Say it with me. Every place on Earth has its own amazing story. Wonderful! Let's read the festival poster. "Welcome to the World 32 Earth Festival! Visit every stand around the oasis. At the climate stand, you can find out why it hardly ever rains in the desert. At the animal stand, you can learn why camels have wide feet. At the graph stand, you can read reports about water and trees. Don't miss the Save Water Corner! Learn how you can save water by turning off the tap. Thank you for exploring the Desert of the Sun with us!" What can you learn at the animal stand? Why camels have wide feet. Is this a fact or an opinion? Every place on Earth has its own amazing story. It's an opinion, and a wonderful one! Suddenly, the Sun Compass shines like the sun itself. Click! The sixth sun crystal drops in. Congratulations! All six sun crystals are shining! The needle spins, then points to the sea. Far away, we see smoke rising from a volcano. It's the Island of Fire! Now, phonics. Let's review. Geography. Geo means earth. Global. Globe plus a, l. Northern. North plus e, r, n. Three million. Three, then two groups of zero zero zero. No s on million. Average. A, g, e sounds like the end of bridge. Goodbye, Fen! Goodbye, Humphrey and Dr. Mira! See you on the Island of Fire!
